Fellowdisciples
FEL-oh-di-SY-plz
n. pl. (those who are disciples together)
Greek summathetes, from sun, together, and mathetes, a learner or disciple. The word occurs once in Scripture, and it is Thomas who speaks to them.

Biblical Definition

Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples, Let us also go, that we may die with him. The setting is the road to Bethany, and the disciples have just tried to talk the Lord out of going: Master, the Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thither again? Thomas does not dispute their assessment. He agrees that the journey is fatal and proposes to make it anyway. The sentence is usually quoted with a note of gloom, and there is gloom in it, but there is also something the church has been slow to credit. This is the man remembered chiefly for doubting, and here he is the one who says go. He is wrong about the outcome — the journey ends not in the disciples' deaths but in Lazarus's raising, and in the declaration, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live. Thomas had the courage and not the expectation. The single occurrence of summathetes is worth noticing too. He speaks not to colleagues but to fellow disciples — learners together under one Master, which is what the word means. Discipleship in the New Testament is never solitary. Thomas proposes a shared death because he already belonged to a shared following, and the Lord's answer to his later doubt was given in that same company, eight days after, with the doors shut.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), under DISCIPLE: a learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.

DISCIPLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.

DISCIPLE, n. A follower; an adherent to the doctrines of another; as the disciples of Plato, the disciples of our Saviour.

FELLOW, n. An associate; a companion; one united with another in the same business or condition.

DIDYMUS, n. A twin; the surname of the apostle Thomas.

LEARNER, n. A person who is gaining knowledge from an instructor, or from books or experience.

Key Scripture

John 11:16 — "Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples, Let us also go, that we may die with him."

John 11:8 — "His disciples say unto him, Master, the Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thither again?"

John 11:25 — "Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:"

Romans 8:17 — "And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together."

Modern Corruption

Discipleship is widely privatised into a solitary spiritual programme; the one occurrence of this word makes disciples plural and mutual, learners together under one Master.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word itself is uncontested; what has been lost is the plural in it. Discipleship is now commonly presented as an individual pursuit — a personal walk, a private devotional regimen, a self-directed course of growth with the church as an optional support. Summathetes assumes the opposite. Thomas addresses men who are learning the same thing from the same Master at the same time, and his proposal is that they go together and, if necessary, die together. The New Testament knows no other kind of disciple, which is why almost every command in the epistles is addressed to a congregation in the plural.

The second matter concerns Thomas himself, and it is a caution about how churches remember people. He is fixed in Christian memory as the doubter, on the strength of one week, and the man who said let us also go, that we may die with him is largely forgotten. Scripture is more balanced than its readers. It records the doubt plainly and it records this, and it records the Lord meeting the doubt with evidence rather than rebuke — reach hither thy finger. A congregation that files its members under their worst recorded moment is doing something the Gospels decline to do.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek summathetes (G4827), a fellow disciple; mathetes (G3101), a learner; Didumos (G1324), Didymus, a twin; sunapothnesko (G4880), to die together with.

expand to see more

Greek summathetes (G4827) — a fellow disciple; its only occurrence in Scripture.

Greek mathetes (G3101) — a learner, one under instruction; the ordinary New Testament word for a Christian.

Greek Didumos (G1324) — a twin; the surname by which John identifies Thomas.

Greek sunapothnesko (G4880) — to die together with; what Thomas proposed.

Greek anastasis (G386) — resurrection; what the journey actually produced.

Usage

"“unto his fellowdisciples” — learners together, the word's only appearance."

"“Let us also go, that we may die with him” — courage without expectation."

"“goest thou thither again?” — the fear Thomas did not dispute."
